why_this_tool: Spark with PySpark lets you practise the whole lesson on a laptop with one engine: lazy DataFrame plans, shuffles and skew, window and Arrow-based feature work, Structured Streaming, and submission to a real cluster manager.
alternatives: Apache Flink is streaming-first with lower latency but a weaker batch and Python story; Dask and Ray Data are Python-native and lighter to operate but have a less mature SQL optimizer and shuffle; DuckDB and Polars are faster on a single machine but do not scale out; managed Spark services run the same engine and trade cluster operations for cost and lock-in.

setup.do: Install a supported Java runtime and Python, then install PySpark with pip into a fresh virtual environment.
setup.done_when: Importing pyspark in the virtual environment's Python and printing its version shows the release you installed.
setup.why: Every later step runs against this local install, and a clean environment keeps the Spark version explicit and repeatable.

setup.do: Download the matching prebuilt Spark distribution and unpack it so the standalone launch scripts and spark-submit are available.
setup.done_when: Running spark-submit with the version flag from the unpacked folder prints the same version as the pip install.

setup.done_when: kubectl lists one Ready node and reports that you are allowed to create pods.

steps.do: Run a PySpark script that creates a SparkSession in local mode and shows a small DataFrame.
steps.done_when: The script prints a table of rows and exits without errors.
steps.why: The SparkSession is the entry point to everything else, and a first run proves that the Java and Python sides can talk to each other.

steps.do: Write a chain of select, filter and groupBy transformations on a larger generated DataFrame, call explain on it, and only then trigger an action such as count.
steps.done_when: The plan prints immediately, and a job appears in the Spark UI only after the action runs.
steps.why: Transformations only build a plan and nothing runs until an action, which is the lazy model behind every cost and correctness question you will debug later.

steps.do: Start a standalone master and one worker on your laptop, then run the same script with its master URL pointing at that cluster.
steps.done_when: The master web UI shows one live worker and your application with an executor assigned to it.
steps.why: With a real cluster manager the driver and the executors are separate processes, so you can see which one plans and which one runs tasks.

steps.do: Create a per-user event table and compute rolling and ranked features over it with window functions, in both the DataFrame API and Spark SQL.
steps.done_when: Each row carries a rank and a rolling aggregate for its user, and both versions return identical results.
steps.why: Window functions are the workhorse of feature tables, and each partition-by clause adds a shuffle you should learn to spot in the plan.

steps.do: Enable Arrow and write a pandas UDF that derives features from a free-text column, then time it against a plain row-at-a-time Python UDF.
steps.done_when: Both UDFs give the same output and the Arrow-based one is measurably faster on the same data.

steps.why: Unstructured data work in PySpark is dominated by the cost of moving rows between the JVM and Python, and Arrow batches are how you cut it.

steps.do: Compare the physical plan and runtime of a join between a large and a small table with and without a broadcast hint.
steps.done_when: The hinted plan shows a broadcast hash join with no shuffle of the large table, and the unhinted run with auto broadcast disabled shows a sort-merge join.
steps.why: Choosing between a broadcast join and a sort-merge join decides whether the large side is shuffled at all, which is the biggest single lever on job cost.

steps.do: Create a join where one key holds most of the rows, run it with adaptive query execution off, then enable the skew join optimization and run it again.
steps.done_when: In the Spark UI the first run shows one task far longer than the rest, and the second run shows the skewed partition split into several tasks.
steps.why: Skewed keys produce one very long task that stalls the whole stage, and you need to recognise that pattern and know the built-in remedy.

steps.do: Run a Structured Streaming query that aggregates events over event-time windows with a watermark and a checkpoint directory, using the built-in rate or file source as the local substitute for a Kafka topic.
steps.done_when: Windowed counts update on every trigger, and after you stop and restart the query it resumes from the checkpoint without recounting old data.

steps.why: On Kubernetes the image is the deployable unit, so the Spark version, Python dependencies and job code are frozen together in it.

steps.do: Write pytest tests with a shared SparkSession fixture that assert DataFrame equality for your feature transformations, and run them from a clean checkout of the pinned environment.
steps.done_when: The suite passes from a fresh environment, and fails with a readable row diff when you deliberately break a transformation.
steps.why: Tests that run on a local session are what let CI catch a broken transformation before it reaches a shared cluster.

steps.do: Deploy the job to your local Kubernetes cluster in cluster mode, with a dedicated namespace and service account and explicit executor counts and resource requests, then read the driver logs.
steps.done_when: A driver pod and the requested executor pods appear in the namespace, the driver pod ends in Completed status, and its logs show the job result.
